statement: In the world's population in 2004, the deaths that one model attributes to alcohol use, compared with nobody drinking, were mostly deaths from injuries, heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer and liver cirrhosis; no paper on file describes acute alcohol poisoning (what happens in the body when someone drinks far too much at once), so that part of the question is not answered here. The model, a comparative risk assessment that applied the alcohol-attributable fractions of WHO's assessments for 2000 and 2002 to WHO's death estimates for 2004 (Rehm et al., 2009), estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, before subtracting the 227 thousand it counted as prevented. Of the deaths caused, 666 thousand were from unintentional injuries (about 27 in 100; the paper's list of categories names road traffic accidents, falls, drownings and poisonings), 545 thousand from heart and blood-vessel diseases (22 in 100), 487 thousand from cancer (20 in 100), 373 thousand from cirrhosis of the liver (15 in 100), 272 thousand from intentional injuries (11 in 100; the list names self-inflicted injuries and violence) and 135 thousand from neuropsychiatric disorders (5 in 100; the list names alcohol-use disorders, depression and epilepsy); injuries of both kinds together came to 938 thousand, about 38 in 100, and men to 2039 of the 2482 thousand, about 82 in 100 (the shares are editors' calculations from the table's rounded thousands). The model attributed 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60 to alcohol, against 3.8 in 100 at all ages, a difference its authors put down mainly to injuries; it prints no causes of death by age. These are a model's estimates, not counted deaths: they come without uncertainty intervals, rest on relative risks from observational studies, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every country, leave out infectious diseases (the authors name pneumonia and tuberculosis), and give no figure for poisoning, which appears only as one of the injury categories. Two narrative reviews add figures that are second-hand: about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with withdrawal delirium die, usually from overheating, heart rhythm disturbances, complications of withdrawal seizures or other illnesses (Schuckit, 2014; see the answer on withdrawal delirium); and people with alcohol use disorders are described as having high death rates, mainly through medical conditions such as liver cirrhosis or injury, with a life expectancy that register analyses in Nordic countries are said to put more than 20 years below the population average, while burden-of-disease reports are said to list alcohol poisoning as the main cause of death under alcohol use disorders (Carvalho et al., 2019, a review that shares an author with the model and gives no figures for poisoning). How many deaths the models attribute to alcohol in all, how the risk of cirrhosis grows with the amount drunk and which cancers go with drinking are separate answers. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How can alcohol kill? One model of deaths around the world in 2004 estimated what the deaths it put down to alcohol were from. Out of every 100, about 38 were injuries (27 accidents, such as road crashes, falls, drownings and poisonings, and 11 self-harm or violence), 22 were heart and blood-vessel disease, 20 cancer, 15 liver cirrhosis and 5 brain and mental health conditions, a group that includes alcohol use disorders. About 82 in 100 were men. Before age 60, the authors say, injuries mattered most. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths: they have no margins of error, lean on studies done mostly in richer countries, and leave out infections. Two reviews pass on other people's figures: about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs (sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal) die, and people with alcohol use disorders have high death rates, mainly through conditions such as liver cirrhosis or injury. No paper on file describes alcohol poisoning itself, that is, what happens in the body when someone drinks far too much at once.
population: The world's population in 2004, as modelled from WHO death estimates by sex, age group and WHO region; and, second-hand through two narrative reviews, hospital patients with alcohol withdrawal delirium and people with alcohol use disorders in a French hospital cohort and in Nordic national registers
exposure: Alcohol use (modelled from recorded and unrecorded consumption per adult and survey-based drinking categories); in the reviews, alcohol withdrawal delirium and alcohol use disorders
comparator: A counterfactual of no alcohol consumption (the model); the population average for life expectancy (review, second-hand); none for deaths in withdrawal delirium
outcome: Deaths attributed to alcohol by broad cause (unintentional injuries, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, cirrhosis of the liver, intentional injuries, neuropsychiatric disorders); deaths among hospital patients with withdrawal delirium and their usual causes; causes of death and life expectancy of people with alcohol use disorders
magnitude: Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004; thousands of deaths, rounded; no uncertainty intervals): deaths caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443), of which unintentional injuries 666 (26.8%), cardiovascular diseases 545 (22.0%), cancer 487 (19.6%), cirrhosis of the liver 373 (15.0%), intentional injuries 272 (11.0%), neuropsychiatric disorders 135 (5.4%), maternal and perinatal disorders 3 (0.1%); unintentional plus intentional injuries 938 (37.8%); men 82.2% (shares are editors' calculations: each row divided by 2482); deaths prevented 227; net share of all deaths 3.8% at all ages and 5.3% under age 60. Schuckit 2014 (second-hand): about 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium die. Carvalho et al. 2019 (second-hand): life expectancy reduced by more than 20 years from the population average in Nordic register analyses. No paper on file gives a figure for deaths from alcohol poisoning.

evidence.extracted: Alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004, in thousands rounded to the nearest thousand: deaths caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443), made up of unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular diseases 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis of the liver 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric disorders 135, maternal and perinatal disorders (low birthweight) 3 and diabetes 0 (fewer than 500); deaths prevented 227 (cardiovascular diseases 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 of 58 738 thousand deaths (3.8%). The table prints shares by sex only and no uncertainty intervals, and has no row for poisoning. Editors' calculation, each total-column row divided by 2482: unintentional injuries 26.8%, cardiovascular 22.0%, cancer 19.6%, cirrhosis 15.0%, intentional injuries 11.0%, neuropsychiatric 5.4%, perinatal 0.1%; the two injury rows together 938 thousand, 37.8%; men 2039 of 2482, 82.2%.

evidence.locator: Identification of disease categories causally linked to alcohol, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The categories the model relates to alcohol: disorders arising in the perinatal period and low birthweight; cancers of the mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver and breast, and other neoplasms; diabetes; alcohol-use disorders, unipolar depressive disorders and epilepsy; hypertensive heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, haemorrhagic stroke and ischaemic stroke; cirrhosis of the liver; road traffic accidents, falls, drownings, poisonings (ICD-10 X40–X49) and other unintentional injuries; self-inflicted injuries, violence and other intentional injuries. The paper does not say which listed categories make up each row of Table 1, and prints no figure for poisonings or for any other single category.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that most of the deaths caused by alcohol were in the broad categories of injury, cancer, cardiovascular disease and liver cirrhosis, and that the deaths prevented were almost entirely cardiovascular; the shares of all deaths attributed to alcohol (3.8%; men 6.3%, women 1.1%) are net of the deaths counted as prevented.

evidence.extracted: 3.8% of deaths in all age groups and 5.3% of deaths in people younger than 60 years were attributable to alcohol (7.9% in men, 1.9% in women); the authors put the larger share at younger ages mainly down to injuries caused by alcohol, with most beneficial effects in older age groups. No breakdown of causes by age is printed.

evidence.extracted: Method: alcohol-attributable fractions combine the prevalence of each exposure category with its relative risk against no consumption, taken from meta-analyses; the fractions for chronic diseases were taken from the comparative risk assessment for 2002 and those for injuries from that for 2000, and take account of drinking patterns for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; the counterfactual is no alcohol consumption, the same for harmful and beneficial effects.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 724 (claim writer), from the PDF

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: more than 25% of global consumption is estimated to be unrecorded and rests mainly on expert opinion; drinking patterns were estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion; the relative risks come from meta-analyses based predominantly on middle-class cohorts in the developed world and are assumed to transfer between countries; no alcohol-attributable infectious disease was included (pneumonia and tuberculosis are named, for the next round); the authors call the uncertainty of the estimates fairly low compared with other risk factors, citing an earlier WHO report, but print no interval for any estimate.

evidence.extracted: Second-hand, in a narrative review: approximately 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients who have withdrawal delirium die (cited to four sources, whose designs and periods are not given), a rate the author says could be reduced by appropriate and timely diagnosis and adequate treatment; death usually results from hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, complications of withdrawal seizures or concomitant medical disorders (cited to two sources).

evidence.extracted: Second-hand, in a narrative review (a Lancet Seminar): alcohol use disorders are associated with high mortality, in the Summary's words mainly due to medical consequences such as liver cirrhosis or injury (the body cites a national retrospective cohort study from France); this excess mortality is said not to be found in burden-of-disease reports, in which alcohol poisoning is the main cause of death listed under alcohol use disorders, but only in special analyses; register analyses in Nordic countries are said to show that the excess mortality can lead to a reduction in life expectancy of more than 20 years from the population average (citing Westman et al., 2015). The Seminar gives no figure for deaths from alcohol poisoning and does not describe poisoning. Its last author (Rehm) is the first author of the model paper cited above.

risk_of_bias.note: The model treats as causal the relative risks of observational meta-analyses that the paper neither shows nor appraises, and it reports no sensitivity analysis (card sc_rehm_2009: editors' checklist, overall high). The two reviews pass on figures whose sources cannot be appraised from them (cards sc_schuckit_2014 and sc_carvalho_2019: overall high).

inconsistency.note: One model gives the breakdown by cause; no second breakdown was read for this answer (a later model, for 2016, is not on file as a PDF and was not used). The reviews speak to other parts of the question.

indirectness.note: Relative risks from studies mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries are applied to every country; drinking is estimated from sales data, expert estimates of unrecorded alcohol (more than a quarter of the total) and surveys; the deaths are for 2004 and the attributable fractions for 2000 and 2002; causes are given only in broad groups, with infectious diseases left out and no figure for alcohol poisoning; the reviews' figures concern hospital patients and people in registers and are second-hand.

imprecision.note: No uncertainty interval for any figure in the model; the reviews give a range and a threshold (1 to 4 in 100; more than 20 years) without intervals or numbers of people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a model or for narrative reviews.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim: which causes of death a model attributes to alcohol, and in what shares. It starts low, as the observational studies behind the model's relative risks do, and is rated down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Descriptive claims are never upgraded. The shares are a model's estimates, not counts, and the statement says so; they are editors' calculations from the table's rounded thousands (each row divided by 2482), so they carry rounding error of a few tenths of a point. Status single study: the breakdown by cause rests on one model (Rehm et al., 2009). The two narrative reviews (Schuckit, 2014; Carvalho et al., 2019) add second-hand figures on other parts of the question (deaths in withdrawal delirium; what people with alcohol use disorders die of) and do not replicate the model; the 2019 review shares an author with it. The claim does not rest only on narrative reviews, because the model supports its main statement, but the reviews' figures are labelled second-hand in the statement. What acute alcohol poisoning does in the body is not answered: no paper on file describes it, the model's table has no row for it, and the statement says so.
